one_liner: Linux heap profiler using LD_PRELOAD and libunwind; much lower time and memory overhead than Valgrind massif (no published numbers).
what_it_does: heaptrack records every heap allocation and free along with its backtrace, so you can find peak memory consumers, leaks, allocation hotspots and temporary allocations. You run `heaptrack <app>` or attach to a running process with `heaptrack --pid` (injection through gdb), and it writes a compressed trace that heaptrack_print (text, massif-format export, flamegraph.pl collapsed stacks) or the Qt/KDE heaptrack_gui analyzes. It replaces massif as a profiling tool, not as an API; no code changes are needed except to annotate custom pool allocators.
how_it_is_fast: The application runs natively instead of on Valgrind's serializing JIT: a preload library interposes malloc, free, calloc, realloc, posix_memalign, aligned_alloc, valloc, dlopen and dlclose, plus mimalloc and Boehm GC hooks, through dlsym(RTLD_NEXT), so only allocation calls pay any cost. Each event captures a backtrace with libunwind's unw_backtrace using a per-thread unwind cache (cache size 1024), deduplicates it into a TraceTree of instruction pointers (sorted children, binary-searched) and emits one compact hex line (+ size index ptr / - ptr) to a pipe. Symbolization and aggregation happen later in the separate heaptrack_interpret process, and a timer thread samples timestamps and RSS from /proc/self/statm.
when_to_use: Heap profiling of large or long-running multi-threaded C/C++ (or Rust/D) applications on Linux that are impractical to run under massif's serialization.
Finding allocation hotspots and temporary allocations (malloc directly followed by free), which massif's pre-aggregated output cannot show.
Attaching to an already running process to see what is allocating right now (needs gdb).
Embedded targets: record a raw trace with --raw on the device and interpret it on a host with --sysroot and debug paths.
CPU-heavy code with few allocations, where heaptrack adds almost nothing because it only intercepts allocator calls.
when_not_to_use: Allocation-heavy hot loops: every malloc/free takes a global lock, unwinds the stack and writes a line, so programs that allocate millions of times per second still slow down noticeably (no overhead numbers are published).

Pool or arena allocators that bypass malloc, or page-level and stack accounting: massif's --pages-as-heap and stack profiling cover these, while heaptrack needs code annotations and cannot profile the stack.
Non-Linux targets: the collector is Linux-only (FreeBSD has code paths); only heaptrack_print and heaptrack_gui build on macOS.
Binaries built with clang's ASan (unsupported), or code linked with old gold linkers, where libunwind produces bogus backtraces that crash the GUI with out-of-memory.
Hour-long captures you need to browse quickly: the data format cannot be seeked, so large profiles load slowly and zooming the timeline reloads them.

integration.dependencies: collector: libunwind (or unwind tables), Boost iostreams and program_options, zlib, optionally zstd, elfutils, libdl, pthread, gdb for attach; GUI: Qt 6.5+, KDE Frameworks, optional KDiagram
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 and CMake 3.16 per CMakeLists.txt (the README's C++11, CMake 2.8.9 and Qt 5 lines are out of date)
integration.platforms: Linux (x86-64, ARM, embedded via --raw); analyzers also build on macOS
integration.thread_safety: Safe for multi-threaded targets: one global timed mutex serializes allocation event recording, and a thread_local RecursionGuard prevents re-entry; pthread_atfork handlers cover forking.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: replaces massif as a workflow (run the app under heaptrack instead of valgrind --tool=massif, and heaptrack_print can export massif format), but it does not do page-as-heap or stack profiling

gotchas: The README's 'multi-threaded applications are not serialized' means the program code; allocator calls from all threads still contend on one global lock inside libheaptrack.
Backtraces need debug symbols and frame unwinding info; release builds without debug info give unresolved frames, and Rust needs debug = true in the workspace Cargo.toml.
The GitHub repo is a mirror: patches go to invent.kde.org/sdk/heaptrack and bugs to bugs.kde.org.
Unwind depth is capped at 64 frames (Trace::MAX_SIZE) and can be lowered for speed; deeper stacks are truncated.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose heaptrack over bytehound when you want a mature, distro-packaged C/C++ heap profiler with a GUI and an attach mode; bytehound claims cheaper unwinding but likewise publishes no numbers. Choose it over memtrail or heapusage when you need full allocation timelines and flame graphs rather than just leak reports.
verified_claims_summary: No measurement exists: the README only says heaptrack's time and memory overhead is 'significantly lower' than Valgrind massif, that it does not serialize threads and that it does not slow non-allocating CPU work. The author's blog post (found by search, not opened) gives only rough estimates, so the tier stays D.
status_note: Actively maintained by KDE and KDAB (version 1.6.80 in CMakeLists, commits through 2026-10-02); the collector is GPL-2.0-or-later with LGPL-2.1+ parts, fine for use as a tool though not for vendoring into proprietary code.
